Inside the movie store on Radio Row, Jeff Bogan stared out the window, wondering how many of the patrons on an August night were what he called normal customers, and how many were shoplifters. Bogan was small and jittery; he was thirty-three, felt fifty, and had trouble remembering a time that he'd felt any younger. At sixteen he had been stealing designer sunglasses from a shop on Lower Greenville and selling them on the street to pay for gas money.

He took full-time at the movie store in '91, after the store manager snatched a part-time gig managing the HOT VIDEO chain at Mockingbird and Oates. Three people came and went below his counter, talking about Steven Roeder, a local actor who'd just been arrested for molesting a fifteen-year-old. Someone said he'd been cracking kids up in the quiet, Fifties-style Strip theater where he worked as an usher. Jeff was startled to see that the temporary manager, Kelly Carmichael, was back behind the till on the other side of the granite counter. Last week she'd asked for a leave of absence, and now she was standing in the lunch break spot he'd staked out six months back when an assistant manager had flaked out.

She turned away to ring up a customer.

He moved back around the counter, out of sight. He'd already decided not to confront her.

Stepping outside the front door, the hot breeze knocked him slightly. The parking lot was nearly empty: the theater across the road, the Film Row, the Angelika Dallas, and the huge new appolachian showed giant's big-budget action movies, and the AMC mocked smaller fare. The driveway at the rest area joins it about three-quarters of a mile north of the bridge. It's a quarter-mile of asphalt that curves around, crosses a little creek, and ends at a dozen paved spaces.

Ray cruised past feeling the edge of the road pull at his tires. As soon as the drive straightens out and there's a clear view of the trucks parked ahead, he saw something wasn't right. The radios of the other trucks were on; the back doors were rattling and the motor of one was running. Something was going on.

But he really didn't see it right away. Sure, there are maybe a dozen rest areas along the east side of I-244, and if you know what to expect you'll find the same thing at every single one: a few trucks, the 24-hour Public Restroom, a picnic shelter with pay phones. These people don't do restaurants or hotel rooms; nothing to clean and no time to wait in line. They sometimes pick up the evening paper or an energy drink. But when nobody's doing that or working on their trucks, it's time to kick back and rest. Same as everywhere else.

The one thing that's always stopping the roadie in mid-solitude is TV. There are satellite dishes up and down, sure, some with the dish on the roof of the truck. That's not cheap. But on a pickup night there's always one big rig with a regular TV antenna out front. Dishes are better and more channels work, but the over-the-counter FM transmitters put out the programs like charm. You can hear the analog from ten miles away. It broadcasts blind and with an FM station on either side piggybacking the program. The program's out there for everybody with a radio in the whole state, and can go on for hours, or until the cops show up. Hell, first night out on my own, the Goddamn thing was pumping from North Nowhere, Arkansas, and kept me company for one hundred miles before I fooled around with the radio and figured out that was why it wouldn't go away.

"Labyrinth," it was, the labyrinth. He remembered saying it aloud. He'd read the word in Kayla's first dictionary, the one for kids, a red hardback printed with black type.

He must have spoken it then, because he remembered turning his head, listening for an answer. WHEN KAYLA CAME home on Saturdays, the smells were what hit her first. Laminated hardwood floors, fresh-ground coffee, stacks of magazines and newspapers that Ray feigned reading, a set of aging golf clubs that he laid out on a card table in the TV room.

There was a downstairs, too, tucked away at the back of the gently sloping lot behind the house, and from the front porch, the pool deck, the playground, it was as if they were alone in the world. But there were neighbors on either side, along with their pools and ranges and two-car garages; teenagers who smoked too much and didn't speak in full sentences; faces she didn't recognize across the fire pit by the lake.

Kayla's dad, Ray, left home early in the morning to deliver perishables for wholesalers and grocery chains across Oklahoma. On good days, he was back by seven or eight, but he rarely ate. Steamed broccoli, grilled chicken, lentil tacos, tinctures that he dropped into his water—Ray believed that whatever ailed him, it was probably his body chemistry, motivated by lack of regular activity and overexertion alternating with overindulgence.

He'd make different faces with all of it—faces Kayla hadn't seen until she went to college. She'd tried telling him that there weren't many body chemistry students majoring in masses and strings, but there wasn't much he hadn't tried. He was going through gut-clear pills and carbs restricted to once a week; more than once, Kayla had woken to find him up in the half-bath, screaming and pushing a seat in place over the toilet. I-44 runs through a hilly, curved open country and the forest-grown, switchbacked mountains of northeastern Oklahoma. The highway is divided, and the area between the lanes is usually flat, though there are stretches where a high ridge or plateau sends up one shoulder of the road and breaks it again thirty feet above the other. They had pulled into the rest area maybe fifteen minutes ago. The parking lot was only about a fourth full. Carol had been nice about it, but the truth was that the truckers here weren't mostly idiots and rule-breakers like he would have thought-they were mostly guys with every possible sticker on their trucks, and family pictures along the visor and stuffed animals and bobbing Jesus or whatever they needed to avoid falling asleep. He wouldn't have minded being a little social, but the thought of talking to anyone new-a tall guy with biceps like beams of light-was just too much. It was cold enough that he'd left the truck idling. His left foot hurt when the brake pedal went numb.

Somewhere in the distance a train went by. Ray had never been on a train before, but he could imagine it was about as dark as space back there. They moved across the farthest edges of this continent like ghosts. He didn't know any of the songs on the radio, so he switched it off and stared out the windows, watching the other trucks, the empty parking spaces, counting down to his nap and then the road home.

At some point there was a knock on his door.

It took Ray a moment to register. They had locked it from the outside to keep him from getting out and wandering into traffic. If it wasn't Carol, who else would knock? He rolled down the window.

Nothing visible. The only light on the lot was the sodium over the doors of the bathrooms. Outside of that, it was nothing but the sky and a pair of cars parked away from the trucks and a figure moving between them.

The figure stopped. It took one look at his truck, the strawberry graphic on the trailer, and it turned and walked away.

Ray hadn't realized how scary it could feel to sit alone in an empty parking lot. He closed the window and turned his head away from the empty space, staring toward the other trucks instead, and felt better.

Ray’s hands tightened on the wheel. People didn’t walk on the interstate, not at one in the morning. Especially not for miles.

He squinted, trying to get a better look. The man seemed… distorted. Like looking through wavy glass. And there was something wrong with the way he moved. A jerky, unnatural gait.

Then, he remembered the strawberries.

He turned his head, straining against the restraints. He had to know.

"The...the strawberries," he croaked. "Are they...okay?"

"Please," Ray said, his voice filled with desperation. "They're supposed to be in Joplin by six. Kayla..."
